periods.analysis: Library Visits per Capita finished 2024-Q3 at 0.45 visits, right on our green target of >=0.45, which tells me residents are still choosing the library as a practical, welcoming place in a very busy summer city. With no prior quarter in this series, I am treating this as our baseline for how the Main, Northgate, Bayfront, and East Harbor branches convert summer reading, cooling-center hours, and family programming into actual access. The strongest operational lift came from the Summer Stories route, where the Bookmobile added Tuesday stops at Pier 6 housing and the Mercado transit plaza, helping visits show up where families already were. This is a green result, but it is not automatic; it reflects staff turning open doors, shade, Wi-Fi, and children’s activities into resident outcomes.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the Q3 baseline by keeping the Summer Stories Bookmobile stops on the 2025 planning calendar and confirming branch staffing for peak afternoon hours at Main and Bayfront. Ask branch managers to review hourly door-count patterns by location, then shift two weekly program slots toward the highest-demand family time blocks. Keep the resident outcome front and center: every added visit should connect people to reading, job search, cooling relief, or school readiness.

periods.analysis: In 2024-Q4, visits rose to 0.53, up 0.08 from 0.45, a strong green quarter and a clear sign that Harborview residents followed the library indoors as evenings got shorter. The increase lines up with Homework Harbor tutoring restarting at East Harbor and Northgate, expanded passport appointments at Main, and the winter concert partnership that brought new families into Bayfront on Saturdays. I especially like that the gain was not just a downtown story; door counters on the L-03 and L-07 entrances showed steady weekend use in neighborhood branches. This quarter broadened the baseline from summer access to year-round usefulness.
periods.recommendations: Lock in the Q4 momentum by renewing the Homework Harbor tutor schedule before the next school semester and reserving Saturday community-room blocks at Bayfront for high-draw civic and family programs. Extend the passport appointment pilot by one additional weekday evening at Main, but track whether it displaces study-room access. Use the Q4 branch-level door-count data to set a simple operating playbook for winter: tutoring, practical services, and warm community programming.

periods.analysis: 2025-Q1 came in at 0.52, down 0.01 from 0.53, still solidly green and essentially holding the higher level we earned in Q4. That small dip is understandable after holiday programming ended and several rain events disrupted evening trips, but residents continued to use the libraries for tax help, Wi-Fi, study rooms, and after-school support. Priya’s test for me is whether a resident could feel the service, and in Q1 they could: the VITA tax-prep tables at Main and the Teen Studio cohort at Northgate kept the buildings purposeful. The arc is encouraging because Q4’s surge did not collapse; it settled into a durable pattern.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green result by pre-booking VITA volunteers earlier and publishing branch-by-branch tax-help hours in the utility bill insert and airport employee newsletter. Extend the Teen Studio model from Northgate to East Harbor for one eight-week cohort, using existing youth-services staff and donated equipment from the Digital Bridge vendor refresh. Watch evening attendance during heavy rain weeks and be ready to add one Bookmobile stop at Harborview Station if fixed-branch visits soften.

periods.analysis: In 2025-Q2, visits moved down to 0.45, a decrease of 0.07 from 0.52, but the measure remained green at the target line. This is the quarter I would call successful but fragile: spring sports, school testing, and the two-week HVAC work at Bayfront reduced casual visits, while staff did the right thing by protecting children’s programming and holds pickup. The fact that we stayed at 0.45 despite Branch Work Order HVAC-BF-214 and a lighter event calendar shows the system has a dependable floor. Still, being exactly at target means we should not drift into summer assuming demand will find us.
periods.recommendations: Treat 0.45 as a green result that needs active stewardship: finish Bayfront’s post-HVAC reopening push with a three-week “Back to Bayfront” program slate and targeted texts to cardholders within one mile. Move pop-up library tables to spring sports sites at Mariner Fields and Civic Park so families see us during the season that pulled them away. Before Q3, confirm Summer Literacy enrollment handoffs so every registered child receives a branch visit prompt and Bookmobile schedule.

periods.analysis: 2025-Q3 improved to 0.47, up 0.02 from 0.45, keeping us green and showing that the summer recovery plan worked. The rebound was modest, but it matters because it came from intentional outreach: Bookmobile Route Blue added Mariner Fields and the Civic Park splash pad, and the Summer Literacy check-in desks converted program participation into branch visits. We also saw practical resident use during hot afternoons, when Main and East Harbor served as cooling spaces with children’s reading corners rather than just places to wait out the heat. After the Q2 low point at the target line, this quarter rebuilt a little operating cushion.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the gain by making Route Blue’s Mariner Fields and Civic Park stops permanent seasonal stops, with a clear July-August staffing plan. Extend the Summer Literacy check-in desk practice into a fall “First Library Card” campaign for kindergarten and sixth-grade transition families. Keep monitoring cooling-day visits separately so we can staff compassionately and still maintain regular circulation, holds, and program service.

periods.analysis: 2025-Q4 rose to 0.54, up 0.07 from 0.47, the strongest quarter in this run and a very healthy green result. The libraries turned summer’s outreach relationships into fall and winter usage through Homework Harbor, the Small Business Desk at Main, and expanded Sunday hours at Northgate funded through the vacancy-savings plan. Residents used the system for real life: homework, language practice, business licensing help, and a safe public place after school. This is the point in the arc where library visits look less like a seasonal spike and more like a trusted civic habit.
periods.recommendations: Protect the Q4 model by continuing Sunday hours at Northgate through the next budget review, with monthly reporting on door count, computer sessions, and program attendance. Extend the Small Business Desk to Bayfront twice per month in coordination with permitting staff and the seaport vendor office. Document the Homework Harbor staffing template now so we can replicate it without scrambling when school resumes after winter break.

periods.analysis: In 2026-Q1, visits eased to 0.51, down 0.03 from 0.54, and remained comfortably green. Some softening after the Q4 high was expected, especially with Sunday holiday closures and weather-related cancellations, but the system retained most of the resident habit we built. The strongest stabilizers were tax assistance at Main, English conversation circles at East Harbor, and the Northgate Sunday schedule, which continued to serve shift workers from the airport corridor. I see this as a healthy normalization, not a retreat, provided we keep our attention on the programs that translate directly into household benefit.
periods.recommendations: Sustain green performance by preserving the Northgate Sunday schedule through the end of Q2 and pairing it with airport-corridor outreach at employee break rooms and transit shelters. Extend English conversation circles with a second weekly session at East Harbor, using trained volunteers and a consistent child-friendly corner. Review canceled program logs from weather weeks and create make-up dates within 10 business days so residents do not lose momentum.

periods.analysis: 2026-Q2 returned to 0.45, down 0.06 from 0.51, still green but again sitting exactly on the target. The pattern now is clear: Harborview can reach strong Q4 peaks and solid Q1 usage, but Q2 needs deliberate programming to avoid sliding below the line as school-year routines break apart and outdoor activities compete for time. This quarter was also affected by the Main Library lobby flooring project, Asset Renewal L-MAIN-FLR-18, which temporarily narrowed the entrance and reduced browsing flow even though holds pickup stayed open. I am glad we held green, and I am equally clear that holding at 0.45 is a prompt to act before summer demand arrives.
periods.recommendations: Stabilize Q2 by scheduling lobby and facilities work outside peak program weeks when possible and by placing a staffed holds-and-signups table near any temporary entrance. Re-launch the pre-summer outreach bundle from 2025-Q3: Route Blue stops, Summer Literacy visit prompts, and pop-up tables at Civic Park and Mariner Fields. Set a watch item for next quarter: if weekly door counts at Main or Bayfront lag the 2025 summer pattern by more than 5%, shift two programs per week into those branches immediately.

periods.analysis: Visits per capita reached 0.46, just above the 0.45 target and up from June’s recorded 0.45. September’s library-card campaign brought new residents into contact with the service, but the visits result leaves little margin.
periods.recommendations: Use the campaign results report to check whether new cardholders return to branches; keep accessible pickup and program options visible during renovation work.
